planting.note: Cold-stratify seed 30-60 days, then sow onto lean, well-drained, sandy or gravelly, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; germination and early growth are slow as the plant builds a deep taproot before it invests much energy above ground.

directions: Plant in lean, fast-draining, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun, avoiding rich or regularly irrigated beds that shorten its life. White beardtongue forms a low clump of narrow gray-green leaves topped by short spikes of pure white, inflated tubular flowers in late spring, a modest-sized counterpart to its larger prairie relatives. Native across the mixed-grass prairies of the central and northern Great Plains, it is a reliable nectar source for bumblebees and small native bees and reseeds lightly once established in open, undisturbed ground.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall for natural winter stratification, or set out divisions in spring, into well-drained sandy or loamy soil in full sun; unlike shade-garden spiderworts, this species wants open, dry prairie conditions and resents heavy wet soil.

directions: Grow in lean, well-drained sandy or loamy soil in full sun; western spiderwort sends up narrow, grass-like, waxy blue-green leaves from a compact clump, with three-petaled blue-violet to rose-purple flowers opening fresh each morning and closing by early afternoon through late spring and summer. It is markedly more drought- and heat-tolerant than the shade-garden Tradescantia species sold in most nurseries, reflecting its origin on dry mixed-grass prairie and sandhills from the Dakotas south through Texas and New Mexico. Divide congested clumps in early spring if flowering declines.

planting.note: Scarify the hard seed coat and sow into lean, well-drained upland prairie soil in full sun; like most prairie legumes it is slow to establish above ground while building a deep, drought-surviving root system.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained upland soil in full sun; silverleaf scurfpea is a bushy, silvery-haired prairie legume with dense, silky foliage that gives the whole plant a soft, frosted appearance even from a distance. Small blue-violet pea-like flowers cluster along the upper stems in early-to-mid summer, followed by small bur-like seed pods, and the silvery leaves make an effective textural contrast against grasses in a native planting. Native to dry upland mixed-grass and tallgrass prairie from the Dakotas and Minnesota south through Kansas and Nebraska, it fixes nitrogen and tolerates poor, rocky soils that few other garden perennials can handle.

planting.note: Dormant-seed in late fall so winter moisture and cold naturally break seed dormancy, into firm, well-drained prairie soil in full sun; this cool-season bunchgrass greens up earliest among native Great Plains grasses each spring.

directions: Sow into firm, well-drained soil in full sun; green needlegrass is a cool-season, mid-height bunchgrass that forms neat, dense clumps of fine blue-green leaves and sends up slender flowering culms tipped with long, twisted, needle-like awns in late spring. It greens up earlier in the season than most warm-season prairie grasses, providing an attractive contrast when paired with big bluestem or switchgrass, and its deep roots make it an excellent soil-stabilizing, drought-tolerant choice for mixed-grass prairie restoration from the Dakotas south to Kansas. Mow or burn in early spring every few years to remove old thatch and encourage vigorous new growth.

planting.note: Nick or scarify the hard seed coat and sow directly where plants are to grow, in loose, deep, sandy soil in full sun; the enormous woody taproot that develops within a season or two makes transplanting established plants essentially impossible.

directions: Direct sow into deep, loose, sandy soil in full sun, since the plant's massive underground taproot makes it impossible to move once established. Despite its genus, bush morning glory does not twine or climb; instead it forms a low, bushy mound of narrow gray-green leaves topped from early to mid-summer with large, funnel-shaped, magenta-pink flowers that open at dawn. Native to sandy prairies, dunes, and roadsides of the central Great Plains including the Nebraska Sandhills, it survives extreme drought by drawing on a taproot that can grow to the size of a large root vegetable over many years, and it needs no supplemental water once established.

planting.note: Set container-grown plants into deep, coarse, fast-draining sandy or gravelly wash soil in full sun; smoke tree needs scarified or hot-water-treated seed to germinate and is slow to reach flowering size, so most gardeners start from nursery stock.

directions: Plant in deep, coarse, fast-draining sandy wash soil in full sun; smoke tree gets its name from the fine, hazy gray-blue branching structure that gives the whole plant a smoky silhouette, especially striking when nearly leafless for most of the year. For a few weeks in late spring the entire canopy fills with small, fragrant, violet-purple pea-like flowers that cover the branches before any new leaves appear. Native to the washes and arroyos of the low Colorado Desert and southeastern Mojave margins of California, Nevada, and Arizona, it depends on periodic deep flash-flood soaking and should never be given regular shallow irrigation, which encourages weak, rot-prone growth.

planting.note: Set out container plants in fall in lean, rocky or sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun; goldenhead establishes best with cool-season root growth ahead of the following spring bloom.

directions: Plant in lean, rocky or sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; goldenhead forms a tidy, rounded mound of narrow pale-green leaves on whitish stems, studded in spring with small, bright golden-yellow, ball-shaped flower heads that stand out against the gray desert pavement it typically grows on. It is exceptionally drought-tolerant and long-lived, native to rocky flats, washes, and slopes across the Mojave Desert of California, Nevada, Arizona, and Utah, and it needs no supplemental irrigation once established beyond its first season. Give it full sun and avoid any rich or regularly watered soil, which quickly leads to rot.

planting.note: Set container plants into lean, rocky or decomposed-granite soil in full sun; Wright's buckwheat needs no seasonal amendment and spreads slowly outward from a low woody base once established.

directions: Plant in lean, rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun; Wright's buckwheat forms a low, sprawling to mounded woody subshrub with small gray-green leaves and wiry stems topped by airy sprays of tiny white to pale pink flowers from summer into fall, aging to attractive rust-brown seed heads that persist through winter. It ranges from the low Mojave Desert up into rocky slopes and washes across California, Nevada, and Arizona, tolerating both intense summer heat and surprisingly cold winter nights at higher desert elevations. It is an excellent nectar source for native bees and small butterflies and needs minimal care once its roots are established beyond the first season.

planting.note: Direct sow onto bare, undisturbed, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun in fall so seedlings emerge with winter rains; desert sunflower will not germinate reliably without this cool, moist winter period.

directions: Direct sow onto bare, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun in fall; desert sunflower is a fast, low-branching annual with grayish, slightly sticky leaves and bright golden-yellow daisy flowers that open in enormous numbers across the Mojave and Colorado Deserts following good winter rains, often carpeting entire hillsides in a classic desert superbloom display. It is one of the most reliable and showy desert annuals to seed into a dry garden, finishing its life cycle quickly before the arrival of summer heat and self-sowing readily in years with adequate rainfall. No supplemental water is needed once seedlings are established.

planting.note: Direct sow onto bare, dry, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun in fall; this smaller desert relative of the California poppy depends on cool winter moisture to germinate and should not be transplanted.

directions: Direct sow onto bare, dry, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun in fall; desert gold poppy is a compact, finely cut-leaved annual, noticeably smaller in every part than the familiar California poppy, with pale lemon-yellow flowers that open on sunny mornings across the Mojave and Colorado Desert floors each spring. It is a common component of desert wildflower seed mixes and superbloom displays, mixing well with desert sunflower and desert bluebell, and completes its entire life cycle in a few short months before summer heat arrives. Once sown, it needs no care beyond occasional light rain or minimal supplemental watering in dry years.
